PARIS, France (CNN)  -- Opposition lawmakers Tuesday ridiculed President Nicolas Sarkozy for taking France back into NATO's military command after more than 40 years, but were unable to stop the move when it came to a vote. French troops on patrol with the Afghan army as part of the NATO mission in Afghanistan. The National Assembly voted in favor of Sarkozy's plan, 329-238. Socialist Laurent Fabius, a former prime minister, told Prime Minister Francois Fillon: "You tell us this would mean more independence and more influence. It would probably mean less independence and less influence." The move did not technically require parliamentary approval, but the president's party scheduled the debate to give opponents a chance to voice their opinions -- and to show a majority backed it. Asking the National Assembly to vote on the issue also showed how sensitive the matter is in France. France was a founding member of the NATO alliance in 1949 but it left the military structure in 1966 amid friction with the United States. "To cooperate is to lose your independence," French President Charles de Gaulle said at the time. For the next 43 years, even though France selectively participated in NATO military operations, de Gaulle's principle remained the governing cornerstone of French foreign policy. If Paris took orders from NATO military commanders, it was reasoned, the nation would no longer have complete control of its destiny. Sarkozy, however, believes the opposite -- that cooperation in NATO is a guarantee of French independence. Rejoining NATO's military command, he argued, will give France a seat at the table for decision-making. From its earliest years, the organization's trans-Atlantic ties were strained because U.S. analysts warned that if the European allies failed to increase their contributions to the alliance, they risked losing the support of the United States, according to NATO. Meanwhile, the European nations felt the United States was trying to dominate the organization, according to NATO. De Gaulle's 1966 decision meant no French forces could be under permanent allied command and that France would have no participation in defense planning. In 1995, France rejoined NATO's military committee, which advises NATO's political authorities on military policy and strategy and provides guidance on military matters to NATO's strategic commanders. While France was still not a part of the military command, it contributed troops and funding to NATO activities, including actions in Kosovo and Afghanistan. Half of all French troops outside the country are assigned to NATO military operations. Opponents of Sarkozy's move -- who include some members of his party -- believe de Gaulle, not Sarkozy, had it right. They started a last-minute petition drive to stop his march back into NATO. "With this decision, France will return as a subordinate country and will lose its ability to represent another image in the world," said Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, a member of the French National Assembly. The president's allies calculate Sarkozy's move will strengthen Europe's hand on defense issues. "There will be more European weight in the way decisions will be made," said Louis Giscard d'Estaing, a member of the National Assembly's U.S. Friendship Committee. "Therefore, the balance of power between the USA and Europe will be re-established within this French move." CNN's Sunaina Karkarey and Jim Bittermann contributed to this report .

PARIS, France (CNN) — Opposition members of parliament mocked President Nicolas Sarkozy on Tuesday over his decision to bring France back into NATO’s integrated military command after an absence of more than four decades, but they failed to block the step in a vote.

The issue was put before the National Assembly, where lawmakers approved Sarkozy’s proposal by 329 votes to 238. The move came as French forces were serving alongside the Afghan army in NATO’s mission in Afghanistan.

Laurent Fabius, a Socialist and former prime minister, challenged Prime Minister François Fillon during the debate, saying: “You tell us this would mean more independence and more influence. It would probably mean less independence and less influence.”

Legally, Sarkozy did not need parliament’s consent to proceed. However, his party arranged the debate so critics could express their objections — and so the government could demonstrate that a majority supported the policy. The decision to seek a vote also highlighted how politically delicate the question remains in France.

France helped create NATO in 1949, but in 1966 it withdrew from the alliance’s military command structure after tensions with the United States. At the time, President Charles de Gaulle summed up his reasoning by saying, “To cooperate is to lose your independence.”

For the following 43 years, France took part in selected NATO military missions, but de Gaulle’s view remained a central principle of French foreign policy. The thinking was that if Paris accepted orders from NATO commanders, France would no longer retain full authority over its own national future.

Sarkozy has taken the opposite position. He argues that participating fully in NATO’s military command will protect French independence by ensuring France has a direct role in shaping decisions.

According to NATO, strains in the alliance’s trans-Atlantic relationship date back to its early period. U.S. analysts warned that if European members did not contribute more, they could lose American backing. European countries, meanwhile, believed the United States was seeking to dominate the organization.

De Gaulle’s 1966 decision meant French troops could not be placed under permanent allied command and that France would not take part in NATO defense planning.

In 1995, France returned to NATO’s military committee, the body that advises NATO’s political leadership on military policy and strategy and gives military guidance to the alliance’s strategic commanders. Even though France still remained outside the integrated military command, it continued to provide troops and money for NATO operations, including missions in Kosovo and Afghanistan.

About half of all French troops deployed abroad are serving in NATO military operations.

Critics of Sarkozy’s decision — including some from within his own political camp — argue that de Gaulle’s approach was correct and Sarkozy’s is not. They launched a last-minute petition effort aimed at halting France’s return to the command structure.

“With this decision, France will return as a subordinate country and will lose its ability to represent another image in the world,” said Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, a member of the French National Assembly.

Supporters of the president believe the move will increase Europe’s influence on defense matters. Louis Giscard d’Estaing, a member of the National Assembly’s U.S. Friendship Committee, said: “There will be more European weight in the way decisions will be made. Therefore, the balance of power between the USA and Europe will be re-established within this French move.”

CNN’s Sunaina Karkarey and Jim Bittermann contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
**French lawmakers approve Sarkozy’s NATO command return plan**

**PARIS, France (CNN)** — France’s National Assembly voted Tuesday to approve President Nicolas Sarkozy’s plan to bring the country fully back into NATO’s integrated military command, reversing a landmark Cold War-era decision by Charles de Gaulle more than four decades ago.

The vote marks a major step in Sarkozy’s effort to realign French defense policy with its NATO allies, particularly the United States, while insisting that France will retain its independent nuclear deterrent and full sovereignty over its armed forces.

Sarkozy has argued that France’s return to NATO’s command structure will give Paris greater influence inside the alliance, rather than leaving it on the sidelines of key military planning. France has remained a member of NATO since the alliance’s founding in 1949, but it withdrew from the integrated military command in 1966 under de Gaulle, who wanted to assert French strategic independence from U.S. dominance during the Cold War.

Opposition lawmakers sharply criticized the move, saying it undermines France’s independent voice in world affairs and risks tying the country more closely to U.S.-led military strategy.

Socialist and Communist deputies accused Sarkozy of abandoning a central pillar of Gaullist foreign policy and reducing France’s ability to act as an independent diplomatic power. Critics also questioned whether the decision would bring France meaningful new influence within NATO or simply symbolize a shift toward Washington.

The government rejected those arguments, saying the global security environment has changed dramatically since de Gaulle’s era. Officials said France already participates extensively in NATO operations, including in Afghanistan and the Balkans, and that returning to the command structure reflects reality while allowing France to shape decisions from within.

De Gaulle’s 1966 withdrawal forced NATO to move its military headquarters from France to Belgium and became one of the defining symbols of France’s effort to maintain autonomy between the United States and the Soviet Union. Although later French presidents gradually increased cooperation with NATO, none had completed the reintegration Sarkozy is now pursuing.

The vote comes ahead of a NATO summit at which France’s return is expected to be formally recognized. French officials have said the move could lead to senior command posts for French officers within the alliance.

Sarkozy has emphasized that France will not surrender control over its troops and will not place its nuclear forces under NATO authority. He has also said France will continue to decide independently whether to take part in military operations.

Still, the decision remains politically sensitive in France, where NATO has long been viewed by many on both the left and the Gaullist right as a vehicle for American influence.

For Sarkozy, the vote represents both a foreign policy milestone and a symbolic break with a decades-old doctrine of distance from NATO’s military leadership. For his critics, it is a retreat from the independence that de Gaulle sought to enshrine in French strategy.

The National Assembly voted **329-238** in favor of the move after a heated debate that exposed deep divisions over France’s role in the Atlantic alliance, relations with the United States and the country’s military commitments abroad, particularly in **Afghanistan**.

Sarkozy has argued that France’s return to NATO’s military command would strengthen the country’s influence inside the alliance while preserving its independence on nuclear deterrence and decisions to deploy French troops. France was a founding member of NATO, but President Charles de Gaulle withdrew it from the alliance’s integrated military command in 1966, seeking to assert French strategic autonomy during the Cold War.

The government linked the vote to a confidence motion, raising the political stakes for lawmakers. Supporters in Sarkozy’s conservative majority said the reintegration would give France a greater voice in NATO planning and leadership, rather than leaving it on the margins of decisions that affect European security.

Opposition Socialists sharply criticized the decision, saying it risked undermining France’s independent foreign policy tradition. Former Socialist Prime Minister **Laurent Fabius** was among the most prominent critics, warning that the move could make France appear too closely aligned with Washington and blur the distinction between French and American strategic priorities.

Several left-wing lawmakers also pointed to the war in **Afghanistan**, where French forces were already deployed as part of the NATO-led mission, as evidence of the dangers of closer integration. They argued that deeper involvement in NATO’s command structure could increase pressure on France to support alliance operations even when they are unpopular at home.

Government ministers rejected that argument, insisting that France would retain full sovereignty over decisions to send troops into combat. They said the return would not place French forces automatically under foreign command, nor would it affect France’s independent nuclear arsenal.

Reaction among French lawmakers reflected the broader debate over national identity and strategic autonomy. Members of Sarkozy’s party praised the vote as a pragmatic modernization of France’s defense posture, saying the old Gaullist arrangement no longer matched the realities of European and trans-Atlantic security. Opposition deputies denounced the decision as a symbolic retreat from the independence de Gaulle had sought to protect.

The vote cleared the way for Sarkozy to formalize France’s return to NATO’s integrated command structure at an alliance summit, where Paris was expected to seek senior command posts in recognition of its renewed role.

France’s reintegration was welcomed by NATO allies, who have long viewed Paris as a major military power whose partial absence from the command structure complicated alliance planning. But at home, the decision remained politically sensitive, reviving a decades-old argument over whether French influence is best exercised from inside the alliance’s command system or from a more independent position outside it.

counterfactuals.output:
**France Returns to NATO Military Command, Reviving Debate Over National Independence**

*PARIS —* France’s decision to rejoin NATO’s integrated military command has reopened one of the most symbolic debates in French foreign policy: how closely the country should align itself with the United States and its European allies without compromising its tradition of strategic independence.

The move, announced by President Nicolas Sarkozy and implemented in 2009, ended more than four decades of French distance from NATO’s military structures. France had remained a member of the Atlantic alliance, but in 1966 President Charles de Gaulle withdrew the country from NATO’s integrated command, arguing that France needed full control over its armed forces and nuclear deterrent.

Sarkozy said the return reflected geopolitical reality. France, he argued, was already one of NATO’s major military contributors, with troops serving alongside alliance forces in the Balkans, Afghanistan and elsewhere. Rejoining the command structure, supporters said, would give Paris greater influence over alliance planning and decision-making rather than leaving it outside the room while still taking part in operations.

“This is not a loss of sovereignty,” backers of the decision argued. “It is a way to increase French influence where decisions are made.”

Under the arrangement, France resumed participation in NATO’s military planning bodies while maintaining control over its nuclear forces. French officials stressed that the country’s nuclear deterrent would remain entirely national and that no French troops could be deployed without the approval of French political authorities.

The decision also brought France senior posts within NATO’s command system, reinforcing the government’s argument that reintegration would give Paris more weight in shaping alliance strategy.

But the issue remains controversial because NATO occupies a particular place in French political memory. For Gaullists, left-wing critics and some foreign-policy traditionalists, France’s partial withdrawal in 1966 was not simply an administrative change; it was a statement that France would not subordinate its defense policy to Washington.

Opponents of reintegration warned that returning to NATO’s military command risked blurring the distinction between French and U.S. strategic priorities. They said France’s independent voice — especially on questions of war, intervention and relations with powers such as Russia — could be weakened if Paris became too closely embedded in alliance structures.

Critics also pointed to France’s opposition to the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003 as an example of why independence mattered. At that time, France’s ability to resist American pressure was seen by many at home as proof that de Gaulle’s policy still had value.

Supporters reject that interpretation. They say France’s return to NATO command does not prevent it from opposing the United States, as sovereignty ultimately rests with elected French leaders. They also argue that European defense ambitions are more credible when France is active inside NATO rather than standing apart from it.

For them, independence is not defined by distance from the alliance, but by the ability to influence it.

Opponents define independence differently. They see it as the capacity to act outside U.S.-led structures when French interests require it. In their view, even if France formally retains control over its troops and nuclear weapons, political and military habits formed inside NATO may gradually narrow France’s room for maneuver.

The dispute reflects a broader tension in French strategy: whether national autonomy is best protected by institutional influence among allies or by preserving visible separation from them.

France’s reintegration did not end that debate. Instead, it reframed it for a new era in which NATO remains central to European security, while France continues to insist that it is not simply another member of an American-led bloc.

counterfactuals.output:
France’s debate over returning to NATO’s integrated military command under President Nicolas Sarkozy centered on sovereignty, Gaullist tradition, France’s global role, and the balance between Atlantic cooperation and European defense.

France was one of NATO’s founding members in 1949, joining the alliance as a central Western European power during the early Cold War. However, in 1966 President Charles de Gaulle withdrew France from NATO’s integrated military command, though not from NATO itself. De Gaulle wanted France to retain full strategic independence, especially over its armed forces and nuclear deterrent, and objected to what he saw as excessive U.S. dominance within the alliance. NATO headquarters and foreign allied forces were moved out of France, and the decision became a major symbol of French sovereignty and “Gaullist” foreign policy.

Despite this withdrawal, France never left the Atlantic Alliance politically and continued to cooperate with NATO. After the Cold War, French forces took part in NATO-led operations in the Balkans, including Bosnia and Kosovo, and later in Afghanistan. By the 1990s and 2000s, France was already deeply involved in NATO missions and planning, even while formally remaining outside the integrated command structure. This made the distinction increasingly symbolic to supporters of reintegration.

Sarkozy argued that returning fully to NATO’s military command would give France more influence inside the alliance rather than less. He claimed that France could better shape NATO strategy from within, while still preserving control over its nuclear deterrent and national military decisions. He also insisted that reintegration would not weaken European defense ambitions; instead, he argued, it could reassure allies that French support for a stronger European defense identity was not anti-American or anti-NATO.

Opponents, including Socialists, Communists, some centrists, and traditional Gaullists, argued that the move abandoned a core element of French independence. They feared it would align France too closely with U.S. policy, reduce its freedom of action, and dilute the legacy of de Gaulle. Critics also questioned what France would gain in practical terms, arguing that it already participated in NATO operations without needing to rejoin the command structure. Some saw the decision as largely symbolic, but symbolically damaging.

The controversy culminated in 2009, when Sarkozy’s government tied the issue to a parliamentary confidence vote. The National Assembly backed the government, clearing the way for France’s full return to NATO’s integrated military command. France received senior NATO posts, including command responsibilities, while maintaining important exceptions: its nuclear forces remained independent, and France did not join NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group.

In essence, Sarkozy presented reintegration as a pragmatic modernization of France’s NATO role, while opponents saw it as a retreat from the independent foreign policy tradition established by de Gaulle.
